settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: XSSFilterImplTest.java:53-56 asserts javascript:alert(1), XML-encoded and percent-double-encoded javascript: forms are rejected by isValidHref
getValidHref falls through to return "" when isValidHref returns false (XSSAPIImpl.java:253-261), so rejected values are dropped rather than emitted
The href regex used (XSSFilterImpl.java:72-80) is the AntiSamy default and explicitly allows only onsite relative patterns plus http/https/ftp/mailto offsite patterns
candidates.description: XSSAPIImpl.getValidHref decodes the input (URLDecoder) and unescapes XML entities, then only percent-encodes " ' > < ` and space. Notably it does NOT encode the ':' scheme separator (except when it appears after a '?'), nor raw control characters (tab, newline, CR, NUL) that browsers strip inside URLs. Therefore the returned sanitized URL may still contain e.g. 'java\tscript:...' or 'javascript:...' forms that are dangerous in an href/src attribute. The only scheme-level protection is the subsequent call xssFilter.isValidHref(encodedUrl), which delegates to the AntiSamy-derived href regexes (onsiteURL/offsiteURL). If those regexes are permissive for any variant, the sanitized value is returned unchanged. This is a defense-in-depth concern: correctness of the href validation hinges on the delegated regex rather than on the sanitizer itself.
missing_evidence: Runtime confirmation that AntiSamy Attribute.matchesAllowedExpression/containsAllowedValue cannot be bypassed with control-char/embedded-scheme variants for the onsiteURL pattern
End-to-end test exercising getValidHref (not just isValidHref) with crafted inputs and observing the emitted value
Browser parsing behavior for the emitted characters
preconditions: A caller uses getValidHref to sanitize an attacker-influenced URL that is then written into an href/src attribute without further context-specific encoding
The delegated isValidHref/onsiteURL regex accepts a scheme value the sanitizer did not neutralize
candidates.title: getValidHref does not explicitly neutralize the URL scheme separator or control characters; scheme blocking is delegated entirely to the AntiSamy/href regex

counter_evidence: The character class deliberately omits 'x' and 'u' and the code comment enumerates them as the disallowed trigger letters (XSSAPIImpl.java:333-340)
A semicolon is not in either character class, preventing breakout of the declaration
Only two whitelist regexes are applied and both must match the whole string, so arbitrary payloads are rejected
candidates.description: getValidCSSColor validates the input against two permissive character classes. The first class [(?i)[#a-fghlrs(+0-9-.%,) whitespace]+] includes letters a-f (hex) but also 'g','h','l','r','s' and, critically, the parentheses '(' and ')' and the 'e' letter (via a-f). The code comment claims critical characters 'x' (expression) and 'u' (url) are disallowed; however allowing letters and parentheses is the minimal set needed to construct the token 'expression(' if the letters needed (e,x,p,r,s,i,o,n) were present - 'e','r','s' are in the class and 'p'/'n' are alphabetically within the named-color branch's [a-zA-Z] class. A value such as an rgba() functional notation is intentionally allowed, so the boundary between allowed function syntax and forbidden CSS functions is not enforced at the character level. If callers place the returned value directly inside a style attribute, legacy/CSS-function execution concerns depend on the consuming browser.
missing_evidence: Whether letters p,n,i,o needed to spell 'expression' can co-occur under the given classes with '(' and ')' and be returned (regex/whitelist evaluation not run)
Browser behavior for the emitted value; modern browsers dropped expression() support
Any caller in this repository that passes untrusted color input
preconditions: Caller writes the returned color value into a CSS context (style attribute or stylesheet) without additional escaping
A browser/CSS engine that evaluates legacy constructs such as expression() is in use
candidates.title: getValidCSSColor accepts character classes containing letters used by CSS function syntax (e.g. 'e', '(', ')')

counter_evidence: The documented threat model for this method is only the multi-line comment end block, per XSSAPI.java:132-140
Any value containing "*/" is replaced by the supplied default
No in-repo caller was found that consumes this value (no call sites in main), so runtime reachability is unproven
candidates.description: getValidMultiLineComment returns the comment unchanged whenever it does not contain the substring "*/". The method performs no filtering of newlines, HTML closing tags (e.g. </script>) or other characters that terminate the containing script/style context. The intended use (per XSSAPI.java:132-140) is inside a <script>...</script> or <style>...</style> block. If a caller wraps the returned value in /* ... */ and the input contains a sequence that closes the surrounding element or otherwise escapes the comment under a specific parser, the guard is insufficient. The classifier only anchors on the single literal "*/".
missing_evidence: A concrete input demonstrating context escape without the literal "*/"
The consuming component's exact embedding/wrapping logic
Whether ESAPI canonicalization (not invoked in this method) would have normalized tricks
preconditions: A caller embeds the returned comment inside a <script> or <style> block
The attacker-supplied comment contains a sequence that terminates the element/context without containing literal "*/"
candidates.title: getValidMultiLineComment only rejects "*/" and performs no other contextual escaping

counter_evidence: XSSFilterImpl.java:104 filters on change.getPath().endsWith(DEFAULT_POLICY_PATH) and only reloads the default handler; the embedded fallback policy is used if the resource is missing (XSSFilterImpl.java:237-253)
setDefaultHandler falls back to DEFAULT_HREF_ATTRIBUTE if no href attribute is defined (XSSFilterImpl.java:273-282), limiting one class of tampering
Repository write access is governed by Sling ACLs not present in this repository, so the threat is speculative here
candidates.description: XSSFilterImpl loads its default AntiSamy policy from resource path 'sling/xss/config.xml' (overlaid under /libs/sling/xss by SLING-Initial-Content), and registers a ResourceChangeListener on that path. On any ADDED/CHANGED/REMOVED event ending with that path, updateDefaultHandler re-reads the policy and rebuilds the handler (XSSFilterImpl.java:101-109, 216-256). This means the content that defines which HTML/attributes are allowed by filterHTML() and check() can be replaced at runtime by writing to that repository location. If an actor with repository write access to that path can modify the policy (e.g. to add permissive attribute regexps or allow script tags), the XSS filtering would be weakened. This is a configuration-integrity concern rather than a code defect.
missing_evidence: Repository permissions/ACLs on /libs/sling/xss and its overlay source path
Whether the content package is read-only at runtime in a default deployment
The default policy path's actual writability in the target installation
preconditions: An attacker has write access to the repository path where the default policy file resides
The ResourceChangeListener fires and updateDefaultHandler reloads the modified policy
candidates.title: Default AntiSamy policy is loaded from a repository path that a ResourceChangeListener will re-load dynamically
